description: Curated public government guidance, kept separate from private scientific source passages. Tips are bounded paraphrases. Requirements apply only within the stated scope; confirm the active funding opportunity, its related notices, and the instructions effective for the submission date.

sources.title: General Grant Writing Tips
tips: Draft the aims early and get feedback before expanding the application.
Match the proposed work to the available time, budget, and team's expertise.
Use the application instructions to structure the outline so reviewers can find the information they need.
Give each paragraph a clear main point, explain unfamiliar terms, and use consistent terminology.
Ask both specialist and less-specialized readers to assess the draft against the opportunity's review criteria.
caveats: NIH presents these writing tips as suggestions; they do not replace mandatory application instructions.
Formatting, attachment rules, and page limits must be checked separately for the chosen opportunity.

sources.title: Advice on Application Sections
tips: Frame aims around scientific goals and expected contributions, rather than a list of experiments.
When feasible, design aims so that a null result still informs the field and leaves a productive path forward.
Use clear subheadings to distinguish rationale, proposed methods, and preliminary studies within the required structure.
Keep experimental plans, budget needs, and bibliography entries aligned as the draft changes.
caveats: Required attachments differ by program; some training applications use a program plan instead of a research strategy.
The page's typical R01 aim count is an example, not a rule for K23 or every research application. Check the current NOFO and application guide.

sources.title: Mentored Patient-Oriented Research Career Development Award (K23)
tips: Explain how supervised research and development will support a clinically trained investigator's commitment to patient-oriented research.
Check which NIH organizations participate in the selected opportunity and whether the project fits a participating organization's mission.
Use the career-development instructions together with the specific opportunity and its related notices.
caveats: This activity-code overview does not establish eligibility or fit for an individual application; the selected NOFO supplies the operative details.
Do not infer clinical-trial eligibility, effort requirements, due dates, or permitted budgets from another K23 application.

sources.title: Individual Career Development
tips: Start the review checklist from Section V of the selected career-development funding opportunity.
Explain why the proposed research and training experience serves the candidate's career-development goals.
Use the appropriate career-development parent announcement to locate the program's baseline review criteria when identifying an opportunity.
caveats: This overview directs applicants to opportunity-specific criteria; it is not a universal K-award scoring rubric.
Mechanisms support different career stages and arrangements. Confirm the selected program rather than generalizing from all K awards.

sources.title: Career Development Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies
tips: Use the candidate section to connect prior experience, future goals, and the specific skills to be developed during the award.
Explain how research and other developmental activities build the capacity needed for the proposed independent career.
For mentored awards, identify each mentor's contribution, supervision, research support, and plan for the candidate's transition toward independence.
Document institutional support and the practical arrangements that provide the effort and resources specified in the opportunity.
Make the research plan achievable and include likely problems and alternative approaches.
caveats: K.100 states that NOFO instructions supersede the application guide. Check related notices and the forms version effective for the submission date.
These selected requirements are not an exhaustive checklist. Some attachments and details apply only to particular career mechanisms.
Subsequent policy notices can supersede the guide: NOT-OD-26-120 removed K-award DMS Plan requirements effective October 5, 2026. Recheck current notices before reusing an older attachment checklist.

sources.title: Applicant Guidance for Simplifying the Review Framework for Most Research Project Grants
tips: Check the activity code and due date before using the simplified research-project review framework.
For covered applications, examine the selected opportunity's application instructions and its review criteria organized into three factors.
Use the opportunity and forms version valid for the actual due date when adapting an older application.
caveats: The published applicability list covers selected research-project mechanisms, including R01, for due dates from January 25, 2025.
K23 and other K awards are not in that list. Do not replace K23-specific review criteria with this framework.

sources.title: Guidance: Rigor and Reproducibility in Grant Applications
tips: Assess strengths and weaknesses in the prior evidence supporting the proposal, including unpublished work, and explain how weaknesses will be addressed.
Describe design, methods, analysis, and interpretation sufficiently to support robust and unbiased results.
Account for relevant biological variables; justify studies restricted to one sex when the NIH expectation applies.
Identify key biological or chemical resources and explain the relevant authentication approach.
caveats: The listed activity codes are a selected retrieval scope for research and mentored career awards, not NIH's complete applicability list.
Consult the current application instructions and NOFO for the appropriate attachments and requirements for the actual study.

sources.title: Resubmission Applications
tips: Confirm that the chosen opportunity permits resubmission and review the prior summary statement before preparing the response.
Use the introduction to summarize substantive changes and address the issues raised in review.
Do not mark revision differences inside application attachments; explain the changes in the introduction instead.
Career-development applicants should arrange the required reference-letter submissions again for a resubmission.
caveats: These are resubmission instructions, not instructions to attach an introduction to a new application.
Check current timing, permitted application types, page limits, and any exceptions in the selected NOFO and related notices.

sources.title: Communicating Research Intent and Value in NIH Applications
tips: Make the title, abstract, and public-health narrative understandable to readers without specialist scientific training.
Explain the proposed work, the problem it addresses, and the potential public-health contribution in direct language.
Retain the technical detail needed for scientific assessment in the research plan and other appropriate sections.
caveats: Plain-language editing should preserve the scientific meaning and uncertainty of the proposal.
The research strategy serves a scientifically literate audience; it need not use the same level of detail as the public narrative.

sources.title: Preparing Your Proposal
tips: Use the applicable Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide alongside the specific solicitation; solicitation instructions may modify the general rules.
For a standard research proposal, distinguish the overview, intellectual merit, and broader impacts in the project summary.
Explain the planned work, its rationale, the method, how success will be assessed, and the potential benefits.
Keep the budget justification, personnel information, available resources, and applicable mentoring and data-sharing plans consistent with the proposal.
caveats: This is NSF guidance and should not be applied as NIH K23 requirements.
The overview is not exhaustive; check the guide and policy updates effective for the proposal date, plus solicitation-specific requirements.

sources.title: NINDS Suggestions for a Good Career Development Plan
tips: Start with career and research goals, identify existing skills and specific gaps, then justify each development activity as a way to close a gap.
Specify how individual and joint mentor meetings will work, and ensure mentor letters agree with that plan.
Demonstrate adequate preparation in experimental design and statistics or explain how the candidate will acquire it.
Avoid unnecessary coursework, poorly matched course levels, and development activities that consume so much time that they undermine the research.
Use successful applications as examples to analyze, while writing a plan tailored to the candidate's own background and trajectory.
caveats: This NINDS advice is not a universal scoring rubric or a guarantee of funding.
The chosen institute and opportunity may have additional or different priorities and instructions.

sources.title: NIA Award Sample Applications and Resubmissions
tips: Use the paired initial submissions, summary statements, and resubmissions to study how applicants revised their scientific and career-development arguments.
Compare the candidate's training needs and research trajectory with the examples before deciding what presentation choices are relevant.
Follow current application instructions and seek feedback on the candidate's own plan.
caveats: These are historical examples from funded applicants, not templates or evidence that a particular style causes funding success.
The catalog describes educational-use conditions and attribution requirements. Review the conditions and each individual sample before copying or redistributing material.
The listing was verified through the official search-index excerpt and NIH's live sample catalog; individual applications were not analyzed here.

sources.title: NIH Sample Applications and Documents
tips: Use the central catalog to find institute-provided funded applications, summary statements, sample plans, and attachment formats.
Study how an example communicates its rationale and methods, then adapt the presentation to the actual science and audience.
Check the sample's mechanism and submission-era forms before using it to structure a new application.
Use official format pages for current attachments instead of assuming that an older successful application's format remains valid.
caveats: Examples are not available for every program and do not replace the current opportunity or application guide.
Follow each sample's attribution and reuse conditions; the catalog does not authorize unrestricted reuse of investigator text, figures, or data.

sources.title: NIH After Review and Next Steps
tips: Read the complete summary statement and identify the scientific issues raised before planning revisions.
Discuss the critiques, possible funding prospects, and next steps with the assigned program official after the summary statement is available.
If funding is unlikely, consider either a substantive resubmission addressing the concerns or a new application with an appropriately revised direction.
caveats: A favorable review is not an award. Funding decisions depend on the institute's process, priorities, and available funds.
Review and funding timelines may vary; use the application status and current NIH communications rather than treating typical intervals as guarantees.

sources.title: Talking to NIH Staff About Your Application and Grant
tips: Before submission, use a brief research description to discuss scientific fit, scope, and the appropriate program with a program officer.
Direct questions about review handling to the scientific review officer during review; discuss interpretation and funding prospects with the program officer after the summary statement is released.
Work with the institution's authorized representative on financial and administrative matters involving grants management.
caveats: The article uses NIGMS examples; identify the staff assigned to the actual institute and application.
Program guidance does not guarantee review scores or funding and is distinct from an authorized award decision.

sources.title: NIH Reference Letters for Career and Fellowship Applications
tips: Confirm whether the funding opportunity requires reference letters and arrange the required number from appropriate referees.
Distinguish confidential reference letters from support letters and mentor statements; sponsors or co-sponsors do not count toward the required references.
Give referees the current instructions, Commons identity, and opportunity number so they can submit directly by the application deadline.
Monitor submission status in Commons and arrange new reference letters for a resubmission.
caveats: Requirements depend on the opportunity. This retrieval scope does not mean every listed award always requires the same number or type of letters.
Applicants can monitor receipt but cannot read the confidential reference letters through Commons.

sources.title: CSR Request a Scientific Review Group
tips: Use the optional Assignment Request Form to express institute or study-section preferences and describe the expertise needed for review.
Compare the proposal's aims and methods with current study-section descriptions and recent related RePORTER awards.
Request relevant expertise rather than naming preferred reviewers; separately explain any potential reviewer conflicts.
Confirm that the requested institute participates in the selected funding opportunity.
caveats: Requests are considered but not guaranteed; some opportunities have a predetermined review location.
Study-section scopes and rosters change. Use the assignment form rather than a cover letter for assignment suggestions.

sources.title: Planned 2027 Updates to NIH Career Development Programs
sources.source_version: NOT-OD-26-098, released August 12, 2026; related DMS notice issued October 5, 2026
tips: For applications planned for due dates on or after October 12, 2027, check the announced consolidated career-award structure and its replacement funding opportunities.
The notice maps current K08 and K23 programs to the future KC1 category; review the final opportunity before adapting an existing K23 application.
Plan separately for the announced future restrictions on using K-award funds for clinical-trial conduct and the route to gaining trial experience through mentors.
caveats: These program-consolidation and clinical-trial changes are prospective, not current K23 submission rules as of the check date. The notice says affected current-code opportunities will expire by July 13, 2027.
DMS changes have a different implementation timeline: NOT-OD-26-120 accelerated that component in October 2026. Do not infer one common effective date for every change.

sources.title: Decision Tool: Am I Doing Human Subjects Research?
tips: Use the decision tool to distinguish research involving interaction or intervention, secondary use of data or specimens, and research involving only deceased individuals.
Document whether specimens or private information are identifiable and whether they were collected specifically for the proposed study.
Resolve the human-subjects determination before choosing the corresponding application responses.
caveats: NIH states that the tool must not be the sole basis for an exemption determination; obtain the appropriate institutional review.
An ex vivo or specimen-based study cannot be classified from its label alone. Specimen source, identifiability, and collection procedures matter.

sources.title: Decision Tool: Does Your Human Subjects Study Meet the NIH Definition of a Clinical Trial?
tips: Assess human participation, prospective intervention assignment, evaluation of the intervention's effect, and a health-related outcome for each proposed study.
For ancillary studies, assess the work in the ancillary study rather than importing the parent trial's classification.
Secondary research limited to existing specimens or health information is distinguished from a clinical trial.
caveats: For due dates from May 25, 2026, qualifying basic experimental studies involving humans are no longer characterized as NIH clinical trials; use the linked BESH guidance.
Minimal risk, a single arm, or healthy participants do not by themselves exclude a clinical trial. Confirm the opportunity permits the actual study type.

sources.title: Implementation of Changes for Basic Experimental Studies with Humans
tips: For covered competing applications with due dates from May 25, 2026, classify qualifying BESH separately from clinical trials.
A BESH-only application can use a Clinical Trial Not Allowed or Optional opportunity unless the opportunity says otherwise; a separate clinical trial changes that choice.
Provide the required human-subjects information, but omit clinical-trial-only fields for BESH unless specifically requested.
caveats: This change does not automatically alter currently funded awards; their established terms continue to govern.
Other applicable requirements remain. Assess the actual study and date; the label basic or mechanistic is not enough to establish BESH status.

sources.title: PHS Human Subjects and Clinical Trials Information: Study Design, Outcomes, and Statistical Power
sources.source_version: FORMS-I; page reports last revised December 2025
tips: Define each important outcome by its priority, measurement, and collection timeframe.
When the statistical-design attachment applies, specify enrollment, expected effects, power, and analysis methods in relation to those outcomes.
Match sample-size and analysis methods to intervention delivery and assignment; clustered designs require appropriate methods.
Keep the study record self-contained while avoiding unnecessary repetition of the research strategy.
caveats: Required fields depend on study classification, mechanism, and NOFO; this is not a requirement to submit a clinical-trial power attachment for every grant.
Check current notices, including the 2026 BESH changes, before applying older form instructions.

sources.title: Protocol Templates for Clinical Trials
tips: Use the NIH/FDA template as an organizational aid for phase 2 or 3 trials requiring an IND or IDE.
Consider the separate behavioral and social science template when the study measures those outcomes or tests a behavioral intervention.
The electronic protocol tool supports shared writing, review assignments, and version control; Word versions are also provided.
caveats: NIH recommends these templates but does not require their use.
The templates have defined study scopes; do not assume either is a mandatory or complete protocol for every study design.

sources.title: Sex as a Biological Variable
tips: For vertebrate-animal and human studies, plan consideration of sex from the research question through design, analysis, and reporting.
Provide scientific justification when proposing to study only one sex, using relevant literature, preliminary evidence, or other pertinent considerations.
Discuss uncertain applicability or design choices with NIH program staff before submission.
caveats: This expectation is conditional on the research; the page does not supply a universal sample-size rule or require every study to be powered for a sex difference.
SABV and the inclusion policies for clinical research are related but distinct requirements.

sources.title: Vertebrate Animals Section
tips: Describe live-animal procedures, species, strains, ages, sex, and numbers for every performance site.
Justify the species and why alternative models cannot achieve the research goals.
Explain pain and distress minimization, postoperative care where relevant, and humane endpoints.
Place scientific justification for animal numbers and biological variables in the Research Strategy; address nonstandard euthanasia justification in the designated supplemental form.
caveats: Applicability includes animals obtained or euthanized for tissue harvest and custom-antibody production.
The VAS does not replace institutional animal-use review, and it must not be used to evade research-strategy page limits.

sources.title: Writing a Data Management and Sharing Plan
sources.source_version: 2026 DMS Plan format; October 6, 2026 genomic-data clarification
tips: For applications subject to a DMS Plan requirement, use the current 2026 format rather than reusing the old narrative template.
Identify expected data types and repositories, sharing timing and duration, justified limitations, and privacy protections.
Address genomic-data expectations where applicable, including both human and non-human genomic data.
caveats: NOT-OD-26-120 removes the DMS Plan requirement for NIH K awards effective October 5, 2026; generic page language should not override that exception.
Whether a plan is required and which sharing obligations apply depend on the mechanism, data, and current notices.

sources.title: Accelerated Implementation of Data Management and Sharing Plan Changes for NIH Career Development (K) Awards
tips: As of this notice, NIH K-award applicants no longer need to submit a DMS Plan.
The change also covers pending applications, pre-award requests, and active K awards, including DMS Plan updates through RPPR.
Use this immediate implementation date when older K-award guidance still refers to an October 2027 change.
caveats: The notice changes the DMS Plan requirement; it does not move the other dates or provisions in NOT-OD-26-098.
Do not interpret removal of a plan attachment as blanket permission to disregard other applicable data-sharing, consent, privacy, or award obligations.

sources.title: Biographical Sketch Common Form
tips: Prepare the NIH Biographical Sketch Common Form and NIH Supplement through SciENcv, which produces the combined submission PDF.
Review transferred information for accuracy and completeness rather than assuming an older biosketch converts correctly.
Check the ORCID and eRA Commons linkage required for the current process.
caveats: The current common form has no downloadable blank template to complete outside SciENcv; an old Word biosketch is not a substitute.
Consult the linked implementation and enforcement notices for the specific submission date and document type.

sources.title: Principles and Best Practices for Protecting Participant Privacy
tips: Assess privacy risks and access controls even when data meet a technical or legal definition of de-identification.
Make future sharing and permitted uses clear in consent and preserve those restrictions when transferring data.
Coordinate institutional review of sharing conditions and communicate them to repositories and downstream users.
caveats: These are principles and best practices; they do not replace applicable laws, consent terms, institutional decisions, or repository agreements.
A determination that a project is not human-subjects research does not by itself settle the privacy risks of sharing its data.

sources.title: Genomic Data Sharing Policy Overview
tips: Assess GDS applicability using the planned scale and type of human or non-human genomic data and any institute-specific expectations.
Plan appropriate repositories, submission timing, and responsible handling of controlled-access data.
For applicable human genomic-data submissions, plan for institutional certification with the responsible institutional officials.
caveats: The overview lists examples and exceptions; an assay name such as RNA sequencing alone does not settle applicability.
Reconcile generic DMS Plan language with current mechanism-specific notices. The K-award DMS Plan exception does not itself establish that a project is outside GDS scope.
